cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Due Process Clause requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before it may permanently terminate the rights of parents in their natural child, so New York's fair-preponderance standard was unconstitutional.
cases.quote: The fundamental liberty interest of natural parents in the care, custody, and management of their child does not evaporate simply because they have not been model parents

relevance.INP-12: Emergency protective custody in Vermont is taken against a constitutionally protected parental liberty interest that survives even allegations of poor parenting, which is the federal floor for any pre-hearing seizure.
relevance.OUT-02: Santosky supplies the constitutional standard of proof that 33 V.S.A. ch. 53 termination proceedings must meet, and Vermont courts apply clear and convincing evidence at termination for exactly this reason.
relevance.FAIL-02: A removal without adequate process is measured against the fundamental parental liberty interest Santosky identifies, which is the substantive premise of § 1983 wrongful-removal claims.
relevance.PMC-06: Any systemic audit of Vermont's chain must test state practice against Santosky's constitutional floor for severing the parent-child relationship.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Servs. of Durham Cty.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Constitution does not require appointment of counsel for indigent parents in every termination proceeding; the trial court decides case by case, subject to appellate review, and no error occurred on these facts.
cases.quote: leave the decision whether due process calls for the appointment of counsel for indigent parents in termination proceedings to be answered in the first instance by the trial court

relevance.OUT-02: Lassiter is the federal floor for counsel at termination; Vermont exceeds it by statute (13 V.S.A. § 5232(3)), as In re C.B. and In re L.H. confirm, so a Vermont parent's counsel claim rests on the statute rather than on Lassiter alone.

cases.holding: SRS (now DCF) owed the reporting children an actionable duty of care because 33 V.S.A. § 4915 imposes mandatory investigative acts for the protection of a particular class, and sovereign immunity did not bar the negligence suit.
cases.quote: Accordingly, we conclude that SRS had a duty to protect plaintiffs under the circumstances of this case.

relevance.INP-01: Sabia holds that the mandatory-investigation statute triggered by a report creates a duty running to the identified children, which is what gives a mandated report legal consequence in Vermont.
relevance.INP-02: A report from any source that identifies particular endangered children can create a special duty of care in DCF, not merely a duty to the public at large.
relevance.INP-06: Reports received through the hotline that identify particular children in danger place DCF under the § 4915 duty Sabia enforces.
relevance.INP-08: The reports in Sabia included disclosures channeled through professionals, and the case establishes that ignoring them exposes the agency to liability.
relevance.INP-10: Sabia turns on DCF's statutory obligation to commence an investigation within the statutory window once a report is received, which is the escalation duty at this node.
relevance.DEC-01: Screening a report out or leaving it unacted upon is not costless in Vermont: Sabia makes the failure to investigate a breach of an enforceable duty.
relevance.DEC-02: Section 4915's mandatory language - investigation 'shall' commence, 'shall' include a home visit and child interview - is the standard Sabia enforces at the accept-for-investigation decision.
relevance.OUT-06: Sabia is Vermont's leading authority permitting damages actions where agency inaction allowed continuing serious harm to a child.
relevance.FAIL-04: It establishes the duty element for suits arising from harm suffered by children known to the agency.
relevance.PMC-04: Sabia shows that Vermont courts will review agency failures to act on known abuse reports, which is the judicial analogue of fatality review.

cases.case_name: Willis S. Sheldon, Individually and as Administrator of the Estate of Dezirae Sheldon v. Nicholas Ruggiero
cases.holding: Summary judgment for a DCF administrative reviewer was affirmed because the mandated-reporter duty under 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a) is triggered only by reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused, and a repetitious allegation adding nothing new did not supply it.
cases.quote: In this context, as a matter of law, defendant did not have reasonable cause to make a report.

relevance.INP-01: Sheldon is Vermont's leading modern decision on when § 4913(a) actually obliges a mandated reporter to report, and it holds the trigger is reasonable cause to believe, judged on what the reporter newly learned.
relevance.INP-02: It clarifies that a third-party allegation that duplicates information DCF already has does not itself generate a fresh reporting duty.
relevance.INP-06: The case measures hotline-level information against the reasonable-cause threshold before any reporting obligation attaches.
relevance.INP-07: Dezirae's injuries came to DCF through a hospital presentation, and the opinion traces how medical findings feed the § 4915 investigation.
relevance.INP-08: Sheldon governs school and agency personnel alike, since § 4913(a) applies uniformly to designated reporters.
relevance.DEC-02: The Court emphasizes DCF's separate statutory obligation under §§ 4915 and 4915b to investigate all potential sources of a child's injuries.
relevance.OUT-06: This is the Vermont child-fatality case defining the limits of individual liability after a death of a child known to DCF.
relevance.FAIL-04: It shows how narrowly Vermont frames personal liability of DCF staff for a death occurring after agency involvement.
relevance.PMC-04: Sheldon is the judicial record of a Vermont child-fatality review and identifies the investigative gap that mattered.

cases.case_name: LaShay v. Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services
cases.holding: A caseworker supervisor was not entitled to official immunity on a claim that he ignored warnings about a foster home where the child was later sexually abused, and SRS waived sovereign immunity to the extent of its liability insurance.
cases.quote: Further, if reporting were mandatory, it was a ministerial, not a discretionary duty.

relevance.INP-01: LaShay holds that where reporting is mandatory it is a ministerial duty, so a Vermont official who fails to report cannot claim discretionary-act immunity.
relevance.ACT-03: The case concerns injury to a child placed in an unlicensed foster home after SRS was warned, and defines agency exposure for placement and supervision failures.
relevance.OUT-06: It permits a damages action for serious harm suffered by a child while in state foster care.
relevance.FAIL-04: LaShay is the Vermont precedent allowing suit against a supervising caseworker and the agency for harm to a child under its supervision.

cases.holding: The Court remanded for ICWA notice to the Mohawk Tribe because the trial court had reason to believe an Indian child was involved, and otherwise affirmed the CHINS merits and disposition orders, holding the preponderance standard governs a CHINS adjudication and that merits and disposition orders must rest on findings of fact.
cases.quote: the standard of proof for a CHINS adjudication is that the findings be supported by a preponderance of the evidence

relevance.INP-04: M.C.P. requires that any court-driven juvenile order rest on timely written findings, which constrains a judge who directs CPS action.
relevance.INP-11: This is Vermont's first ICWA decision; it requires the court itself to notify a tribe once it has reason to believe an Indian child is involved, and it construes the 'Indian child' and 'Indian tribe' definitions.
relevance.DEC-05: It fixes the burden the State carries once a CHINS petition is filed and opens the dependency case.
relevance.ACT-02: M.C.P. also reviews a disposition order that conditioned reunification on the parents' admission of abuse, framing the Fifth Amendment limits on court-ordered services.

cases.holding: A CHINS adjudication was affirmed because the merits inquiry is directed at the child's welfare rather than each parent's individual fitness, which is addressed at disposition, and the State's burden is a preponderance of the evidence.
cases.quote: The focus of the CHINS proceeding was on B.R.'s welfare; the question of father's fitness to parent B.R. will be addressed at disposition.

relevance.DEC-05: B.R. is the controlling statement of what the State must prove when it files a CHINS petition, and of the child-centered focus of the merits stage.
relevance.ACT-02: It locates the assessment of each parent's fitness and service needs at disposition rather than at merits, which is where court-ordered services are set.

cases.case_name: In re A.O. & I.O., Juveniles & In re B.G. & E.G., Juveniles
cases.holding: The CHINS merits and disposition orders for four children were reversed and vacated as unsupported by the findings or the record, and the orders allowing a party's advocate to inspect the other children's juvenile records without a need-to-know designation were reversed.
cases.quote: We therefore reverse the CHINS merits determination as unsupported by the findings or the record.

relevance.DEC-05: The case shows that a CHINS petition must be proved as to the circumstances existing when it was filed, and that domestic violence by one adult plus later non-engagement with DCF is not automatically enough.
relevance.ACT-05: It examines whether a mother's safety planning and separation from an abuser sufficed, which is the practical alternative to removal at this node.
relevance.OUT-05: Reversal of the merits determination vacates the case, the clearest Vermont example of a CHINS proceeding ending for failure of proof.
relevance.FAIL-01: A.O. & I.O. is a recent, published reversal of both the agency-sought adjudication and the resulting disposition.
relevance.FAIL-06: The opinion reverses orders that released confidential juvenile records to a party's advocate without the statutory need-to-know designation.
relevance.PMC-05: It marks the statutory limits on disclosure of juvenile-case records under 33 V.S.A. § 5117, which bounds any transparency request.

cases.holding: The CHINS determination was reversed because the evidence did not support the ground the State pleaded, and the Court declined to reach the disposition order transferring custody to DCF.
cases.quote: For these reasons, we reverse the family division's determination that J.N. was CHINS.

relevance.DEC-01: J.N. demonstrates that conduct that does not in fact establish lack of proper parental care should not have generated an adjudication, reinforcing rigorous screening.
relevance.DEC-05: The State must prove the specific CHINS ground alleged in its petition and cannot have the adjudication upheld on an alternative theory.
relevance.OUT-05: Reversal ends the case, illustrating dismissal for unproven allegations.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is a published reversal of an agency-sought CHINS adjudication for insufficient evidence.

cases.holding: Parents' appeal from a CHINS adjudication was dismissed as moot because the family division's jurisdiction terminated when unconditional, unsupervised custody was returned at disposition, and no mootness exception applied.
cases.quote: We conclude that this case does not present a live controversy or fall within a recognized exception to the mootness doctrine and therefore grant the State's motion to dismiss.

relevance.DEC-06: M.M. describes the conditional custody order route that keeps a child at home with DCF-arranged services instead of a removal.
relevance.ACT-01: It shows how a service and safety plan can be carried out under a conditional custody order rather than by compulsion following removal.
relevance.ACT-05: The conditional custody order in M.M. functioned as a protective order that secured firearms access and mental-health services without removing the child.
relevance.ACT-06: The case turned on the parents' resistance to recommended mental-health services for a child expressing suicidal and homicidal ideation.
relevance.OUT-01: Return of unconditional, unsupervised custody at disposition is the reunification endpoint, and it terminates the family division's jurisdiction.
relevance.OUT-04: M.M. fixes when Vermont juvenile jurisdiction ends, which is the starting point for any question about continued DCF involvement with an older youth.
relevance.OUT-05: Once custody is returned and jurisdiction ends, the case is over and an appeal of the underlying adjudication is moot.

cases.holding: A post-disposition order transferring custody of a child back to DCF is a final appealable order, and the preponderance standard, not clear and convincing evidence, governs it because the deprivation is temporary rather than a permanent severance.
cases.quote: In its decision to modify the plan to transfer legal custody of I.B. back to DCF, therefore, the trial court here applied the proper standard of proof.

relevance.INP-04: The case begins with a CHINS petition accompanied by a request for an emergency care order, and traces the judicial steps that follow.
relevance.INP-12: I.B. distinguishes the lower proof required for temporary state custody from the clear and convincing showing required for permanent severance.
relevance.DEC-04: It confirms that an emergency care order and later temporary transfers rest on a preponderance standard in Vermont.
relevance.ACT-03: I.B. governs the proof and findings required when a court moves a child into or back into DCF foster custody after disposition.

cases.holding: A disposition order continuing DCF custody was affirmed; the trial court had discretion to decline new evidence on a relative's suitability where it had recently taken extensive evidence on that question, and could rely on its earlier findings.
cases.quote: mother's rights were not violated by the court's decision not to hear additional evidence of grandmother's suitability

relevance.INP-04: A.M. defines the evidentiary control a judge retains over disposition proceedings in a CHINS case.
relevance.ACT-02: It sets the standard of review for a disposition order and case plan, including the concurrent goals the plan may carry.
relevance.ACT-04: A.M. is the Vermont authority on how a relative's suitability for placement is litigated and re-litigated in the CHINS case.

cases.holding: The Human Services Board's reversal of a registry substantiation was itself reversed and remanded because the Board must apply the same substantiation standard DCF applies under its Policy No. 55 rather than a different standard of its own.
cases.quote: we hold that the Board should have used the standard embodied in Policy No. 55 and must do so on remand

relevance.INP-02: R.H. shows that a single reported incident can support substantiation if it meets the risk-of-harm definition in 33 V.S.A. § 4912(4).
relevance.INP-10: It explains the statutory chain from report to investigation to substantiation and registry entry.
relevance.DEC-01: The decision defines what a report must show before DCF may substantiate rather than close it out.
relevance.DEC-03: R.H. is the leading Vermont case on the substantiation standard and on the Board's obligation to apply it consistently on de novo review.
relevance.ACT-05: The opinion addresses the interplay between a family-court abuse prevention order and registry substantiation arising from the same conduct.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the Supreme Court reversing an administrative reversal of DCF, showing review runs in both directions.

cases.holding: The substantiation and registry placement were reversed because they had to be supported by sufficient evidence known to DCF at the time of substantiation, and the petitioner's later admissions could not retroactively justify them.
cases.quote: However, after-acquired evidence cannot salvage a substantiation that was not supported by sufficient evidence in the first place.

relevance.INP-06: The report in K.R. came from an emergency-room nurse, and the case fixes how much such a report must establish at the moment DCF acts on it.
relevance.INP-07: A hospital report of a parent's overdose triggered the investigation, and K.R. limits how far that medical information can carry a finding.
relevance.DEC-01: K.R. requires the record at the time of the decision to support the finding, which is the discipline that separates a sound screening call from a defective one.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the controlling limit on substantiation: the finding must stand or fall on the evidence DCF had when it made the determination.

cases.holding: The Human Services Board's reversal of a risk-of-harm substantiation was vacated and remanded because the Board recited evidence instead of making the written findings of fact that 3 V.S.A. § 3091(c) requires.
cases.quote: The Board failed to meet this obligation here. Its mere recitation of the evidence does not suffice.

relevance.INP-10: The case sets out the statutory path from mandatory investigation under §§ 4915-4916 to a registry record and the definitions of abuse, neglect and risk of harm.
relevance.DEC-03: M.G. and K.G. requires that any administrative decision confirming or rejecting a substantiation rest on express written findings, not a summary of testimony.

cases.holding: The good-cause standard for accepting a late appeal from a registry substantiation looks only to why the appellant missed the deadline, not to the strength of the underlying substantiation.
cases.quote: We hold that the good cause standard is applied when determining whether the offender at issue had a valid reason for failing to meet the appeals deadline

relevance.INP-08: M.S. arose from substantiated abuse by a high-school instructional aide and coach, the classic school-setting disclosure.
relevance.DEC-03: It governs whether a person substantiated and placed on the Child Protection Registry can still obtain review after missing the statutory appeal deadline.
relevance.PMC-03: The case defines the practical accessibility of Vermont's administrative review mechanism for registry decisions, which is what an independent review body would be assessing.

cases.holding: Summary judgment applying collateral estoppel to a registry substantiation was reversed because the Human Services Board could not inspect the related CHINS file without a need-to-know designation from the family court under 33 V.S.A. § 5117(b)(1)(F), and the stipulated facts did not establish what the substantiation required.
cases.quote: A need-to-know designation from the family court was required before the Board could inspect the contents of the juvenile files in question.

relevance.INP-09: H.H. limits what an oversight or adjudicative body may see in juvenile-court files absent an express judicial designation.
relevance.DEC-03: A CHINS stipulation does not automatically preclude a parent from contesting a substantiation and registry placement arising from the same events.
relevance.FAIL-01: The decision reverses an administrative ruling that had foreclosed a parent's challenge to DCF.
relevance.FAIL-06: It identifies the statutory gate that controls transfer of confidential juvenile records between Vermont bodies.
relevance.PMC-03: The case shows the evidentiary constraints under which Vermont's administrative review of DCF decisions must operate.
relevance.PMC-05: H.H. is the Vermont authority on the need-to-know designation required before juvenile-case records may be inspected outside the case.

cases.holding: The termination case was remanded for notice to the Bureau of Indian Affairs because the court itself had a duty to give ICWA notice once information in a court-ordered evaluation gave it reason to believe the children were of Indian ancestry.
cases.quote: We conclude that the trial court had a duty to provide notice once it had reason to believe the children were of Indian ancestry.

relevance.INP-11: J.T. places the ICWA notice duty on the Vermont family court, not only on the petitioning party, and triggers it on information already in the court's own record.

cases.holding: No ICWA notice was required where the asserted tribes, the Abenaki and Micmac, are not federally recognized, and excluding non-recognized tribes from ICWA does not violate equal protection.
cases.quote: we agree with the court's conclusion in T.I.S. that the ICWA exclusion of non-recognized tribes does not violate the Equal Protection Clause

relevance.INP-11: This is the decisive Vermont case for practitioners, because the tribes most often asserted in Vermont, the Abenaki and Micmac, lack federal recognition and therefore do not trigger ICWA.
relevance.FAIL-05: A.J. rejects an equal-protection challenge to the federal-recognition line, which is the framework for any claimed tribal or ancestry-based discrimination in a Vermont child-welfare case.

cases.holding: The family division had reason to know K.S. might be an Indian child once a parent reported Cherokee heritage on the record, but after notice was given and the tribes responded, the determination that K.S. was not an Indian child was affirmed along with the termination order.
cases.quote: father's statement was sufficient to give the court reason to know that K.S. was an Indian child for purposes of the ICWA

relevance.INP-11: K.S. applies the 2016 federal ICWA regulations in Vermont, holding that a participant's statement of tribal heritage anywhere in the record, including a permanency case plan, triggers the inquiry and notice duty.

cases.holding: Termination was affirmed; a reasonable-efforts finding is a separate determination from the best-interests inquiry and is not a precondition to terminating parental rights, although the level of assistance given to parents remains relevant to whether they can resume parenting in a reasonable time.
cases.quote: the court is not required to find DCF made reasonable efforts as a prerequisite to termination

relevance.OUT-01: C.P. explains that the adequacy of DCF's reunification assistance bears on whether a parent can resume parental duties within a reasonable time.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the controlling Vermont rule that a deficient reasonable-efforts record does not by itself defeat a termination petition.
relevance.FAIL-03: C.P. separates the federally driven reasonable-efforts finding from the state-law merits of termination, so a federal compliance lapse does not automatically invalidate the state outcome.
relevance.PMC-01: The reasonable-efforts determination C.P. describes is the judicial finding that federal reviews and Title IV-E funding depend on.
relevance.PMC-06: C.P. is the clearest statement of the structural gap between federal reasonable-efforts compliance and state termination outcomes in Vermont.

cases.case_name: In re D.F., H.F., M.F. and D.F., Juveniles
cases.holding: Termination of the father's rights was affirmed notwithstanding his completion of case-plan tasks, and his separate challenge to the standalone reasonable-efforts finding was dismissed as moot once termination was upheld.
cases.quote: A reasonable-efforts finding is essential to preserving federal funding for state child-welfare programs.

relevance.ACT-02: D.F. holds that completing every task in a case plan does not compel a finding that a parent can resume parenting, which is the limit of court-ordered services as a defense.
relevance.OUT-01: It addresses a father's claim that expanded visitation would have enabled reunification and explains why the trial court could still find stagnation.
relevance.FAIL-03: D.F. identifies the reasonable-efforts finding under 33 V.S.A. § 5321(h) as the mechanism preserving federal funding, and holds a parent's challenge to it moot once termination stands.
relevance.PMC-01: The opinion ties the Vermont reasonable-efforts hearing directly to 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), the federal performance requirement.
relevance.PMC-02: It is the Vermont Supreme Court's own statement that these judicial findings exist to protect the federal funding stream, which is what a financial audit would trace.

cases.holding: Termination based in part on a father's extended pretrial incarceration was affirmed, because the court must assess individually how the incarceration, pretrial or not, affects that child's best interests rather than treat incarceration as an automatic ground.
cases.quote: Our statutory imperative requires the family court to review the individual circumstances of each child to determine how a parent's incarceration—whether pretrial or not— affects the child's best interests.

relevance.OUT-02: M.W. is Vermont's leading authority on terminating the rights of an incarcerated parent and forbids treating incarceration itself as dispositive.
relevance.FAIL-05: It answers the claim that terminating on the basis of pretrial detention penalizes a presumptively innocent parent, requiring an individualized best-interests analysis instead.

cases.holding: Termination was affirmed: an ADA noncompliance claim is not a defense to a termination petition because the ADA does not directly apply to such proceedings, and a stipulation limiting SRS's recommendations had no greater force than a judgment and was modifiable on changed circumstances.
cases.quote: We conclude that the ADA does not directly apply to TPR proceedings.

relevance.DEC-06: B.S. shows that a negotiated, service-based arrangement between the agency and parents remains subject to modification when circumstances change.
relevance.ACT-01: The written agreement placing mother and child together at a family center is the paradigm of a voluntary service arrangement, and B.S. defines its legal weight.
relevance.OUT-02: It forecloses the argument that inadequate disability accommodations bar termination, directing parents to raise ADA complaints separately and promptly.
relevance.FAIL-05: B.S. is the controlling Vermont answer to disability-discrimination claims raised against DCF in a termination case.

cases.case_name: In re L.H., L.H. and L.H., Juveniles
cases.holding: Termination orders were reversed and remanded for a new hearing because the lawyer who had represented the children then represented the State in the same matter, creating an unwaived conflict of interest that prejudiced the parents.
cases.quote: we conclude that a conflict of interest by the State's counsel compromised the proceedings

relevance.OUT-02: L.H. holds that a termination judgment cannot stand where the State's lawyer previously represented the children in the same case.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the leading Vermont example of a court vacating a termination outcome for a structural fairness defect rather than for evidentiary insufficiency.

cases.holding: Termination was affirmed: appointed counsel's prior adoption of a child from DCF did not create a disqualifying conflict, and the Court referred to its rules committee the question of what procedure would govern ineffective-assistance claims in termination cases.
cases.quote: the court did not abuse its discretion in denying father replacement counsel on this basis

relevance.FAIL-01: K.F. sets the Vermont standard for attacking a termination order on grounds of conflicted or ineffective counsel, and notes that no procedure yet exists for adjudicating such claims.

cases.holding: The family court properly refused to vacate a termination order: 33 V.S.A. § 5113(b) does not reach termination orders even while an appeal is pending, and relief under § 5113(a) and Rule 60 was within the court's discretion to deny.
cases.quote: we again reaffirm that § 5113(b) does not apply to a termination order, even if that order is currently the subject of an appeal

relevance.OUT-02: C.L. is the controlling Vermont rule on the finality of a termination order and forecloses reopening it on changed circumstances.

cases.holding: Denial of a mother's motion to set aside a termination order was affirmed, because fraud on the court requires a showing of conscious wrongdoing and an intent to deceive, which was absent, and changed-circumstances relief is unavailable against a termination order.
cases.quote: Mother's motion to set aside the termination order was appropriately denied.

relevance.OUT-05: G.L. defines the narrow circumstances in which a closed Vermont juvenile case can be reopened for misconduct by DCF, and holds that misstatements without intent to deceive are not enough.

cases.holding: Termination was affirmed; while a CHINS case is pending the probate division cannot adjudicate a minor guardianship petition, but the family division may do so after transfer under 14 V.S.A. § 2624(b), and father's unpreserved objection to the absence of a relative suitability assessment failed.
cases.quote: while a CHINS case is pending, the probate division does not have jurisdiction to adjudicate the minor guardianship petition

relevance.INP-05: C.B. maps where a relative's own guardianship petition must be filed and heard once DCF is already involved with the child.
relevance.DEC-06: It shows the guardianship route as an alternative to a DCF-custody outcome, though it must be pursued in the family division once a CHINS case is open.
relevance.ACT-04: C.B. sets out DCF's duty under 33 V.S.A. § 5307(e)(5) to identify relatives and complete suitability assessments, and holds the objection must be preserved at the temporary-care hearing.
relevance.OUT-03: The case establishes that the family division, not the probate division, decides a minor guardianship once a CHINS case is pending.

cases.case_name: In re Appeal of T.O. & L.O.
cases.holding: The Human Services Board lacked jurisdiction over grandparents' claim that DCF failed to comply with state and federal relative-placement requirements; their remedy lies in the family division of the superior court, and no due process violation resulted.
cases.quote: That procedure is access to the family division, not to the Human Services Board.

relevance.INP-09: T.O. & L.O. fixes the boundary of the Human Services Board's oversight jurisdiction over DCF conduct in an open CHINS case.
relevance.ACT-04: It catalogues DCF's relative-identification, notification and suitability duties under 33 V.S.A. § 5307 and 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(29) and identifies the only forum that can enforce them.
relevance.OUT-03: Relatives seeking placement or permanency must pursue party status or a guardianship petition in the family division rather than an administrative appeal.
relevance.FAIL-03: The case addresses alleged non-compliance with federally conditioned relative-notice requirements and holds the administrative forum unavailable to remedy it.
relevance.PMC-01: The relative-notice obligations at issue are conditions on federal child-welfare aid, making this the Vermont decision on their enforceability.
relevance.PMC-02: It shows that failures to meet federally funded placement conditions are not redressable through Vermont's administrative fair-hearing system.
relevance.PMC-03: T.O. & L.O. defines what Vermont's independent administrative review body may and may not examine in DCF casework.
relevance.PMC-06: The case exposes a structural accountability gap between federal relative-placement mandates and available Vermont remedies.

cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of S.O. (L.O. and T.O., Appellants)
cases.holding: Dismissal of grandparents' guardianship petition without a merits hearing was affirmed because, once parental rights were terminated and residual rights transferred to DCF, 14 V.S.A. §§ 2626 and 2627 gave them no right to a consensual or nonconsensual guardianship.
cases.quote: we conclude as a matter of law that grandparents are not entitled to a consensual or nonconsensual guardianship under the plain language of 14 V.S.A. §§ 2626 and 2627

relevance.INP-05: S.O. shows the statutory limits on a relative's own petition for guardianship once DCF holds custody and rights have been terminated.
relevance.ACT-04: It marks the point after which kinship placement can no longer be pursued through the guardianship statutes.
relevance.OUT-03: S.O. is the controlling Vermont authority on when guardianship is and is no longer available as a permanency route for relatives.

cases.holding: Denial of the grandfather's petition to terminate parental rights was affirmed, but the refusal to terminate the voluntary guardianship was reversed and the case remanded to transfer custody of the child to her fit father.
cases.quote: Once the court made findings supporting the denial of the termination of parental rights petition, there was no reason not to return K.M.M. to her fit parent

relevance.INP-05: K.M.M. arises from a voluntary guardianship the parents themselves entered, and shows how that consensual arrangement is later unwound.
relevance.ACT-01: It defines the legal consequences of a parent's voluntary placement of a child with a relative and the parent's right to end it.
relevance.OUT-01: K.M.M. holds that once the parent is found fit, the child must be returned without further evaluation or delay.
relevance.OUT-03: It applies the constitutional rule that a third party cannot keep custody over a fit parent on a bare best-interests comparison.

cases.holding: A fifteen-year-old in DCF custody was in custody for Miranda purposes when questioned by police at his foster home, so the resulting statements were suppressed and the trial court judgment reversed.
cases.quote: We conclude that the juvenile was in custody, and therefore reverse the trial court judgment.

relevance.INP-03: E.W. governs police questioning of a child in state custody and the role of an 'independent interested adult' when the foster parent is the adult present.
relevance.DEC-02: It constrains how investigative interviews of a child in DCF custody may be conducted in the placement setting.
relevance.ACT-03: The case defines the rights a child retains inside a foster placement when the state questions him there.
relevance.OUT-04: E.W. addresses the legal status of an older youth in DCF custody, the population whose continued care and rights are at issue at this node.

cases.case_name: Elizabeth Lawson v. Patricia Halpern-Reiss and Central Vermont Medical Center
cases.holding: The Court recognized a common-law private right of action for a medical provider's unjustified disclosure of treatment information, but affirmed judgment for the hospital because the disclosure fell within the exception for mitigating an imminent and serious threat.
cases.quote: no reasonable factfinder could determine that the disclosure was for any purpose other than to mitigate the threat of imminent and serious harm to plaintiff and the public

relevance.INP-01: Lawson defines when a Vermont clinician may disclose patient information to authorities without incurring liability, the civil backdrop to the mandated-reporter duty.
relevance.INP-07: It is the controlling Vermont authority on the scope and limits of a medical provider's disclosure of treatment information to third parties including law enforcement.
relevance.ACT-06: The decision frames the imminent-and-serious-harm standard that justifies acting on, and disclosing, clinical information in an emergency.

cases.case_name: Toensing v. Attorney Gen. of Vt.
cases.holding: Records produced or acquired in the course of agency business are public records under the Public Records Act even when they sit in employees' private accounts, and where a requester specifically seeks such communications the agency must ask the named employees to produce them.
cases.quote: the PRA's definition of "public record" includes digital documents stored in private accounts, but emphasize that it extends only to documents that otherwise meet the definition of public records

relevance.INP-09: Toensing determines what agency material an outside investigator or oversight body can actually obtain from DCF and other Vermont agencies.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the leading Vermont decision on an agency's search obligations under the Public Records Act and therefore on what counts as a disclosure failure.
relevance.PMC-02: Financial and audit records held by state officials are reachable under the PRA even in personal accounts if they meet the public-record definition.
relevance.PMC-05: Toensing is the controlling Vermont analogue to FOIA for records requests directed at state child-welfare agencies.
relevance.PMC-06: It establishes the documentary reach of any independent analysis of Vermont agency conduct.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: Triable issues existed on the parents' procedural due process claim and the child's Fourth Amendment unreasonable-seizure claim arising from her removal from school without a court order, although the defendants retained qualified immunity because the rule was not clearly established in 1990.
cases.quote: where there is reasonable time consistent with the safety of the child to obtain a judicial order, the “emergency” removal of a child is unwarranted

relevance.INP-12: Tenenbaum is the governing Second Circuit rule for Vermont on when protective custody may be taken without prior judicial authorization.
relevance.DEC-04: It holds that the mere possibility of danger is not enough: emergency circumstances mean the child is immediately threatened with harm and there is no time to get an order.
relevance.ACT-03: Removing a child into state care implicates the child's own Fourth Amendment right against unreasonable seizure, not only the parents' due process rights.
relevance.FAIL-02: Tenenbaum is the controlling circuit precedent defining an unlawful removal for § 1983 purposes in Vermont.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: Agency lawyers who initiate and prosecute child-protective proceedings have absolute immunity from § 1983 claims, but caseworkers do not, because their removal decisions are the functional equivalent of an arrest; on these facts the caseworkers were nevertheless protected by qualified immunity.
cases.quote: The caseworker defendants are not entitled to absolute immunity on plaintiffs § 1983 claims because their actions were the functional equivalent of arresting officers in criminal cases.

relevance.INP-03: Cornejo treats a caseworker's removal decision as fundamentally a police function, which is why the law-enforcement standards govern it.
relevance.INP-12: It confirms that the official who takes a child into protective custody is subject to the ordinary objective-reasonableness test rather than absolute immunity.
relevance.DEC-04: The decision fixes the immunity framework applicable to the emergency-removal decision itself in the Second Circuit, which includes Vermont.
relevance.FAIL-02: Cornejo is the Second Circuit's controlling allocation of absolute and qualified immunity in § 1983 wrongful-removal litigation.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: Summary judgment for the defendants was affirmed because during the relevant period the newborn was held by the hospital for medical reasons rather than by the child-welfare agency, so no Fourth or Fourteenth Amendment violation arose from the retention.
cases.quote: Mora was held by the Hospital for medical reasons, not concerns about possible parental mistreatment and CWA policies

relevance.INP-07: Kia P. separates a medical hold arising from a positive newborn toxicology screen from state child-protective custody, which determines which constitutional rules apply.
relevance.INP-12: It shows that not every hospital retention of a child amounts to a state seizure triggering protective-custody analysis.
relevance.DEC-04: The case marks the point at which continued retention becomes an agency removal decision requiring constitutional justification.
relevance.ACT-06: Kia P. is the Second Circuit authority on emergency medical retention of an infant and the limits of agency responsibility for it.
relevance.FAIL-02: It defines a boundary of § 1983 liability, since a genuinely medical hold is not an unlawful removal.

cases.holding: Denial of the mother's motion to modify and vacate a termination order was affirmed; the Court held that although the State's initial burden to terminate residual parental rights is clear and convincing evidence, a parent moving under 33 V.S.A. § 659(a) to modify or vacate that order need show changed circumstances only by a preponderance, absent an intervening adoption.
cases.quote: It is settled law that a state's initial burden of proof in seeking to terminate residual parental rights is by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.OUT-02: T.E. is the Vermont source of the clear-and-convincing standard the State must satisfy to sever the parent-child relationship permanently, and it also fixes the lesser burden a parent bears when later moving to modify or vacate that termination order.
relevance.OUT-01: The opinion measures a parent's claim to resume care against whether she can do so within a reasonable amount of time rather than 'in the near future,' which is the operative reunification inquiry.

cases.holding: Termination was affirmed; the Court held that suspension of parent-child contact under 33 V.S.A. § 5319(a) is a temporary deprivation that may be sustained on a preponderance showing that the suspension is necessary to protect the child's physical safety or emotional well-being, so no clear-and-convincing finding of unfitness was required at that stage.
cases.quote: state intervention which effects only a temporary deprivation of parental rights requires a lesser showing of proof by a preponderance of the evidence

relevance.DEC-04: B.C. is the primary Vermont authority for the rule that state action working only a temporary deprivation of parental rights, including emergency and interim custody orders, is governed by the preponderance standard; In re I.B. quotes this case for that proposition.
relevance.ACT-03: It states the proof required to keep a child in DCF placement and to curtail parent-child contact during that placement, grounding that authority in 33 V.S.A. § 5319(a).

cases.case_name: Estate of Sumner v. Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services
cases.holding: Summary judgment for the Department was affirmed because no reasonable jury could find that its alleged negligence in supervising and placing a CHINS youth proximately caused that youth's rape and murder of his seven-year-old cousin; the youth's independent criminal act was an intervening cause the Department had no duty to anticipate.
cases.quote: In this case, a reasonable jury could not have concluded that the Department had a duty to anticipate Steven's rape and murder of Crystal Sumner.

relevance.OUT-06: Sumner is the counterweight to Sabia at this node: a child died in circumstances traceable to a placement the agency knew had collapsed, yet no liability followed because the fatal act was not foreseeable to the agency.
relevance.FAIL-04: It marks the outer limit of Vermont's special-duty doctrine, holding that agency inaction is not actionable where the harm came through an unforeseeable independent criminal act by a person under agency supervision.
relevance.ACT-03: The case arose from a disposition order leaving legal custody in the Department while the child lived at home and then with a relative, and it defines agency exposure for failing to seek modification once that placement failed.

cases.holding: Termination of the father's residual parental rights was affirmed, but the Court held that the most critical best-interests factor — whether the parent will be able to resume parental duties within a reasonable period of time — is forward-looking, and that parents must be judged on their conduct rather than on psychological test results.
cases.quote: the inquiry required by § 5540(3), which we have repeatedly emphasized as the most critical factor in a termination-of-parental-rights case, is forward-looking

relevance.OUT-02: B.M. supplies Vermont's substantive termination analysis, which the rest of this layer lacked: the two-step changed-circumstances-then-best-interests framework, the stagnation test, and the requirement that the court assess the parent's prospective ability instead of treating an earlier period as dispositive.
relevance.ACT-02: It holds that a parent's late but genuine compliance with services does not by itself defeat a stagnation finding, and asks whether the improvement substantially conformed with the expectations set at CHINS adjudication and in the agency's case plan.

cases.case_name: Southerland v. City of New York
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: Summary judgment for the caseworker was vacated on the Fourth Amendment unlawful-search claims arising from a family-court entry order obtained through allegedly false statements, on the procedural due process claims, and on the children's Fourth Amendment unlawful-seizure claim, because qualified immunity could not be resolved as a matter of law on that record; summary judgment was affirmed only on the father's substantive due process claim.
cases.quote: the Children's right not to be taken from the care of their parent without court order, parental consent, or emergency circumstances was firmly established

relevance.INP-12: Southerland is the leading modern Second Circuit statement, binding in Vermont, that a child may not be taken into protective custody absent a court order, parental consent, or genuine emergency circumstances.
relevance.DEC-04: It holds that a caseworker who procures the warrant-equivalent family-court entry order through knowingly false or misleading statements loses the presumption of reasonableness that order would supply, so the entry and removal are judged on a corrected record.
relevance.FAIL-02: With no Vermont decision on warrantless CPS entry, this is the controlling authority for a § 1983 claim built on a caseworker's entry obtained by false statements and the removal that followed, and it holds qualified immunity unavailable at summary judgment on such a record.

cases.case_name: W.H. v. Department for Children and Families
cases.holding: Refusal to register an Alabama order awarding the father sole custody was affirmed because Vermont had already commenced and was exercising jurisdiction over the juvenile in conformity with the UCCJEA as her home state, so Alabama could not simultaneously exercise jurisdiction and neither the UCCJEA nor the PKPA obliged Vermont to recognize its order.
cases.quote: The simultaneous-jurisdiction provision of the UCCJEA precludes a court from exercising jurisdiction if a proceeding "has been commenced in a court of another state having jurisdiction" under the UCCJEA.

relevance.DEC-05: W.H. is Vermont's authority on which state may open and keep a dependency case when an out-of-state parent holds or seeks a competing custody order, and it confirms that CHINS, neglect and termination proceedings are 'child custody proceedings' under the UCCJEA.
relevance.INP-11: This is the layer's only interstate-jurisdiction decision: it applies the federal Parental Kidnapping Prevention Act together with 15 V.S.A. §§ 1061-1096 to decide whose courts control a child already in DCF custody.

cases.holding: Termination of the mother's rights was reversed because the family division found the material change in circumstances by a preponderance rather than by clear and convincing evidence, and the ruling that the court lacked jurisdiction over the father, a Sri Lanka resident who had never been to Vermont, was also reversed, with both cases remanded.
cases.quote: The court's determination of whether there has been a material change in circumstances must be by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.OUT-01: R.W. fixes at clear and convincing evidence the State's proof of stagnation, the failure of parental capacity that forecloses reunification and opens the door to termination.
relevance.OUT-04: In a footnote applying 33 V.S.A. § 5103(c) the Court states that the family division's jurisdiction will end when the seventeen-year-old child turns eighteen; that observation is dictum but is the closest Vermont appellate statement of when juvenile-court oversight of an aging-out youth stops.
relevance.INP-08: The case entered the child-protection system through the older child's disclosure of sexual abuse to her school guidance counselor, the paradigm educational-disclosure pathway.

cases.case_name: Tina Stocker v. State of Vermont
cases.holding: Judgment as a matter of law for the State was affirmed: the only non-discretionary DCF duty supporting a damages action is the 33 V.S.A. § 4915 duty to record a report and make an initial determination whether it is valid, assessment and investigation under §§ 4915a and 4915b are discretionary and within sovereign immunity, and plaintiffs could not show the recording failures proximately caused the children's continued abuse.
cases.quote: any implied right of action against DCF based in this statutory scheme is limited to violations of mandatory duties pursuant to § 4915

relevance.DEC-01: Stocker is the modern Vermont limit on liability for screening decisions: DCF must record a report and decide whether it is valid, but its judgment whether the report meets the § 4912 definition of abuse is discretionary and immune.
relevance.DEC-02: It separates the mandatory acceptance decision from the discretionary conduct of the assessment or investigation under §§ 4915a and 4915b, and holds the Legislature foreclosed any private right of action as to the latter.
relevance.INP-10: The case traces how a report must be recorded and screened before an investigation duty attaches, and substantially narrows Sabia's escalation duty as the statute now reads.
relevance.FAIL-04: Stocker is Vermont's most recent decision on agency liability for prolonged abuse of children repeatedly reported to DCF, and it requires causation to be proved against the narrow recording duty alone.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the current Vermont ceiling on damages actions for serious harm to children known to DCF and should be read with Sabia and Sumner as the third point of the special-duty line.
relevance.PMC-04: The opinion is the judicial record of a Vermont serious-harm review, cataloguing dozens of unrecorded reports and identifying exactly which agency failures are and are not remediable.

cases.holding: The delinquency adjudication was reversed and the juvenile's statements suppressed because, under Chapter I, Article 10 of the Vermont Constitution, a juvenile may waive counsel and the privilege against self-incrimination only after an opportunity to consult privately with an informed adult who is independent of the prosecution, and the state-contracted group-home director was not such an adult.
cases.quote: Although our prior cases apply only to waivers in court, we now hold that the same principles apply to police interrogation of juvenile suspects.

relevance.INP-03: E.T.C. is the foundational Vermont rule governing police contact with children, requiring an independent interested adult before any juvenile waiver, and it arose from state troopers questioning children who were in SRS custody in a state-contracted group home.
relevance.DEC-02: It constrains how an investigative interview of a child may be conducted, holding that a caretaker aligned with the agency or urging cooperation with police cannot serve as the child's independent adviser and that the consultation must be private.

notes: Vermont has NO intermediate appellate court. The Supreme Court of Vermont (CourtListener court_id 'vt') is the only appellate court, so the usual highest-court-then-intermediate ladder collapses to a single tier here. Every Vermont case in this brief is a published opinion of the Supreme Court of Vermont (precedential_status 'Published' on CourtListener); no unpublished memorandum decisions were used. In re A.J., 169 Vt. 577, 733 A.2d 36 (1999), is a published three-justice entry order (mem.) rather than a full signed opinion; it is included because it is the only Vermont decision squarely holding that ICWA does not reach the Abenaki and Micmac, which is dispositive in most Vermont ICWA inquiries, and because it is reported in the official Vermont Reports.

Every case listed was retrieved from the CourtListener v4 API in this session and its opinion text was read. Each quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text after normalizing whitespace and curly quotation marks. All quotes are from majority/lead opinions; the concurrence in In re M.E. and the dissents in In re K.R., In re B.R., In re D.F. and the Southerland en banc denial were read and deliberately excluded.

DATE CAVEAT: CourtListener's date_filed for the two U.S. Supreme Court clusters is wrong. It reports 1982-02-22 for Santosky v. Kramer and 1981-08-28 for Lassiter. The opinions themselves state 'Decided March 24, 1982' and 'Decided June 1, 1981'. This brief uses the true decision dates (1982-03-24 and 1981-06-01); a consumer reconciling against the CourtListener cluster metadata should expect a mismatch on those two records only.

The pre-existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the VT node files are keyword-matched noise (Act 250 land-use appeals, utility petitions, hospital budget orders, guardianship-of-adults cases). None was retained. Three titles were checked and did survive as genuine on-point authority under their correct captions: In re Guardianship of S.O. (2021 VT 89) and In re Appeal of T.O. & L.O. (2021 VT 41), which are the two halves of the same grandparents' fight over S.O., and the registry line of cases. 'In re Vermont Permanency Initiative, Inc.', 'In re Appeal of H.D.', 'In re G.B.', 'In re N.S.', 'In re A.K. and P.K.' and 'In re J.D. and C.D.' were not verified as on point and were dropped.

GAPS - DEC-06 (Differential/Alternative Response): Vermont operates a two-track Family Services response under DCF Rule 2000, but no published Vermont Supreme Court decision construes the alternative-response track itself. DEC-06 is mapped to the nearest analogues: In re C.B. (guardianship as a non-DCF-custody route), In re M.M. (conditional custody order keeping the child at home with services) and In re B.S. (negotiated voluntary service agreement and its modifiability). A lawyer should treat DEC-06 as governed by statute and rule, not case law.

GAPS - OUT-04 (Extended Foster Care / Aging Out): there is no published Vermont appellate decision construing extended foster care, transition-age-youth services, or 33 V.S.A. sec. 5103(c) in the CHINS/foster-care context. The three cases mapped are the closest available: In re M.M. (when family-division jurisdiction terminates), In re S.D. (age-limited exclusive jurisdiction under sec. 5103, decided in the delinquency context, and also overruling In re F.E.F. on the State's right to appeal) and In re E.W. (rights of an older youth living in a DCF foster placement). Practitioners should rely on 33 V.S.A. ch. 53 and DCF Rule 7000 directly.

GAPS - FAIL-03 (Federal Compliance Failure), PMC-01 (CFSR) and PMC-02 (OIG/Single Audit): no Vermont or Second Circuit decision adjudicates a CFSR finding, a Title IV-E funding penalty, or a Single Audit Act deficiency involving Vermont DCF. These nodes are mapped to the Vermont cases that actually construe the federally driven requirements: In re D.F. (the sec. 5321(h) reasonable-efforts finding exists to preserve federal funding under 42 U.S.C. sec. 671(a)(15)), In re C.P. (that finding is not a prerequisite to termination) and In re Appeal of T.O. & L.O. (relative-notice conditions under 42 U.S.C. sec. 671(a)(29) are not enforceable through the Human Services Board). The absence of private enforcement is itself the finding for these nodes.

GAPS - PMC-03 (Citizen Review Panels) and PMC-04 (Fatality Review): no Vermont case construes CAPTA sec. 5106a(c) citizen review panels or a Vermont child-fatality review commission. These nodes carry the cases that define the reach of the review bodies Vermont does have - the Human Services Board (In re Appeal of T.O. & L.O.; In re Appeal of H.H.; In re M.S.) - and the three Vermont fatality/serious-harm damages cases (Sheldon, Baptie, Sabia).

GAPS - Fourth Amendment caseworker entry and home searches: there is no published Vermont Supreme Court decision on a CPS caseworker's warrantless entry into a home. The governing authority is Second Circuit: Tenenbaum v. Williams and Cornejo v. Bell. Southerland v. City of New York, 681 F.3d 122 (2d Cir. 2012), is the leading modern Second Circuit statement on caseworker entry obtained by false statements to a family court and was read in full; it is NOT included as a case entry because CourtListener's only text for that panel opinion carries embedded line numbers throughout, so no quotation of the required length can be produced as an exact substring. Counsel relying on this layer for a caseworker-entry claim should read Southerland directly.

ICWA in Vermont is unusual and this is the single most important practical point in the layer. Under In re A.J. the Abenaki and Micmac - the tribes most often asserted by Vermont families - are not federally recognized and therefore do not trigger ICWA, and the exclusion survives equal-protection review. ICWA still applies where a federally recognized tribe is implicated: In re M.C.P. (Mohawk) required remand for notice, In re J.T. placed the notice duty on the court itself, and In re K.S. applies the 2016 federal regulations at 25 C.F.R. sec. 23.107. Vermont has no state ICWA statute and no case law on qualified expert witnesses, active efforts or the sec. 1915 placement preferences - if those issues arise, there is no Vermont authority and counsel must argue from the federal statute, the regulations and out-of-state persuasive authority.

Standards of proof in Vermont run on three levels and the layer reflects them: preponderance at CHINS merits and at post-disposition custody modification (In re M.C.P.; In re B.R.; In re I.B.), the DCF 'reasonable person would believe' standard for registry substantiation (In re R.H.; In re M.G. and K.G.), and clear and convincing evidence only where the State seeks to sever the parent-child relationship permanently (In re I.B., citing In re T.E.; Santosky v. Kramer).

Vermont's registry line (In re R.H., In re M.G. and K.G., In re K.R., In re M.S., In re Appeal of H.H.) is the richest body of Vermont child-welfare case law and should be treated as the backbone of DEC-03. Note the practical asymmetry: the Supreme Court has reversed the Human Services Board for being too lenient toward parents (R.H., M.G. and K.G.) and reversed DCF for substantiating on an inadequate record (K.R., H.H.).

Right to counsel: Vermont parents' counsel right in juvenile proceedings comes from 13 V.S.A. sec. 5232(3) and is broader than the federal case-by-case floor in Lassiter (see In re C.B. and In re L.H.). As of In re K.F. (2013) the Vermont Supreme Court had not decided whether parents in termination cases have a legal right to EFFECTIVE counsel, and referred to its rules committee the question of what procedure would apply; no later published decision found in this session resolves it. This is an open question a Vermont practitioner should flag.

Not found in Vermont published case law, after targeted searches: sibling placement or sibling-contact rights; children missing or absent from foster care; extended foster care benefits; differential response; child-fatality review commissions; retaliation against reporters or foster parents. Searches for each of these in court=vt returned either no results or only off-point matches.

API usage: approximately 100 CourtListener requests, paced at one every two seconds, with no 429 responses. Search hits were used for metadata (cluster_id, citations, court, date, opinion ids) and full opinion text was pulled only for candidates actually evaluated; cluster endpoints were called only to confirm slugs, date_filed and precedential status for the 40 selected cases.

Missing (for a later pass): In re T.E., 155 Vt. 172, 582 A.2d 160 (1990) — verified to exist on CourtListener (cluster 8209176). The brief's own notes rely on it ("In re I.B., citing In re T.E.") as the Vermont source of the clear-and-convincing standard for permanent severance, yet it appears nowhere as a case entry. It should anchor OUT-02 and the proof-standard contrast at INP-12/DEC-04 rather than being carried indirectly through I.B.

Missing (for a later pass): In re B.C., 2013 VT 58, 194 Vt. 391, 81 A.3d 1152 — verified to exist (cluster 1043603). This is the decision In re I.B. actually quotes for the rule that "intervention which effects only a temporary deprivation of parental rights requires a lesser showing of proof by a preponderance of the evidence." It is the primary authority for DEC-04 and ACT-03 and the brief cites only the case that quotes it.

Missing (for a later pass): Estate of Sumner v. Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services, 162 Vt. 628, 649 A.2d 1034 (1994) (mem.) — verified to exist (cluster 2102878). It is the express counterweight to Sabia, holding the child-protection agency had no duty to anticipate a sexual assault and murder perpetrated by a child under its supervision, and Baptie itself contrasts the two. A brief that maps Sabia to FAIL-04 and OUT-06 without Sumner presents only the plaintiff-favorable half of Vermont's special-duty doctrine.

Missing (for a later pass): In re B.M., 165 Vt. 331, 682 A.2d 477 (1996) — verified to exist and verified to be a termination-of-parental-rights decision (Johnson, J.; father's rehabilitation after substance abuse against five years of foster placement). More broadly, OUT-02 as constructed contains no case at all stating Vermont's substantive best-interests analysis under 33 V.S.A. sec. 5114 or the stagnation/changed-circumstances test; every mapped case addresses a collateral issue (proof standard, counsel, incarceration, reasonable efforts, finality). That is the largest doctrinal hole in the layer.

Missing (for a later pass): Southerland v. City of New York, 681 F.3d 122 (2d Cir. 2012) — the brief identifies it as the leading modern Second Circuit statement on a caseworker's entry obtained by false statements to a family court, says it read the opinion in full, and then omits it solely because CourtListener's text carries embedded line numbers that defeat exact-substring quoting. That is a tooling artifact, not a legal reason. With no Vermont decision on warrantless CPS entry, Southerland should be a case entry at INP-12, DEC-04 and FAIL-02 with a shorter quotation or a paragraph-level pin cite.

Missing (for a later pass): W.H. v. Department for Children and Families, 2020 VT 104 — verified: a published Vermont Supreme Court decision holding that Vermont need not register an Alabama custody order for a juvenile already in DCF custody under a Vermont order, applying the UCCJEA (15 V.S.A. secs. 1061-1096) and the PKPA. The brief has no interstate-jurisdiction or ICPC authority anywhere in the chain, and a practitioner handling a Vermont DCF case with an out-of-state parent or order would expect this case.

RESOLVED 2026-09-21 — all six authorities named by the verifier were searched for, retrieved from CourtListener in this session, read in full, and confirmed real and on point. Nine cases were added in total (the six named plus three found while closing thin nodes), bringing the layer to 47 cases. The six 'Missing (for a later pass)' notes above are retained verbatim as the audit trail for this pass; each is now answered by a corresponding 'Added' note below.

Added In re T.E., 155 Vt. 172, 582 A.2d 160 (1990) (cluster 8209176) for OUT-02 and OUT-01: it is the Vermont source, previously carried only indirectly through In re I.B., of the rule that the State's initial burden to terminate residual parental rights is clear and convincing evidence, and it separately fixes the preponderance burden a parent bears on a 33 V.S.A. sec. 659(a) motion to modify or vacate a termination order absent an intervening adoption. It was NOT mapped to INP-12 or DEC-04 as the verifier suggested, because the opinion's only emergency-custody content is a one-line recital of the 1980 emergency detention order and it states no rule for pre-hearing seizures; In re B.C. carries that contrast instead.

Added In re B.C., 2013 VT 58, 194 Vt. 391, 81 A.3d 1152 (cluster 1043603) for DEC-04 and ACT-03: it is the primary authority for the temporary-deprivation/preponderance rule that In re I.B. merely quotes, and it applies that rule to suspension of parent-child contact under 33 V.S.A. sec. 5319(a) during DCF custody. It was not mapped to INP-12, which is already at the six-case ceiling with stronger seizure authority.

Added Estate of Sumner v. Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services, 162 Vt. 628, 649 A.2d 1034 (1994) (mem.) (cluster 2102878) for OUT-06, FAIL-04 and ACT-03: it is the defense-side counterweight to Sabia and LaShay, and any practitioner given only the plaintiff-favorable half of Vermont's special-duty doctrine would be misled. IMPORTANT CORRECTION to the verifier's description: the Court did not hold that no duty existed. It affirmed summary judgment on PROXIMATE CAUSE, reasoning that the youth's independent, intentional criminal act was an intervening cause the Department had no duty to anticipate, and it expressly declined to rest on the duty-of-care ruling below. The holding and quote in this entry track the proximate-cause rationale, not a no-duty rationale. Sumner is a published three-justice entry order (mem.) in the official Vermont Reports; no full signed Vermont opinion covers this point.

Added In re B.M., 165 Vt. 331, 682 A.2d 477 (1996) (cluster 8209472) for OUT-02 and ACT-02: this closes what the verifier correctly called the largest doctrinal hole in the layer. B.M. states Vermont's substantive termination framework — the two-step changed-circumstances-then-best-interests analysis, the stagnation test drawn from In re M.M. and In re H.A., the rule that the 'reasonable period of time' inquiry is forward-looking and cannot be satisfied by declaring that a reasonable period expired years earlier, and the rule that parents must be judged on conduct rather than on psychological test scores. Note that B.M. construes 33 V.S.A. sec. 5540, the predecessor of the current sec. 5114 best-interests criteria; the four factors were carried forward substantively unchanged.

Added Southerland v. City of New York for INP-12, DEC-04 and FAIL-02, with a CITATION CORRECTION: the leading panel opinion is 680 F.3d 127 (2d Cir. 2012) (cluster 800656, opinion 800656, Sack, J.), not 681 F.3d 122. Cluster 799761 / 681 F.3d 122 contains only the order denying rehearing en banc plus the Raggi and Jacobs dissents from that denial — which is the text the prior pass read and correctly excluded. The line-number problem was likewise a text-version artifact: CourtListener's html_lawbox rendering of opinion 800656 is clean, and the quote in this entry was machine-verified as an exact substring of it. Note 9 above is therefore superseded on both points; a Vermont caseworker-entry claim now has a mapped circuit authority.

Added W.H. v. Department for Children and Families, 2020 VT 104 (cluster 4808108) for DEC-05 and INP-11: it is the layer's only interstate-jurisdiction authority, holding that Vermont's simultaneous exercise of UCCJEA home-state jurisdiction over a child in DCF custody bars registration of a competing Alabama custody order and that neither the UCCJEA nor the federal PKPA requires recognition. Mapped to INP-11 because that node covers federal jurisdictional triggers and the PKPA analysis is federal; readers should understand the node otherwise concerns ICWA and tribal jurisdiction. Vermont still has NO published appellate decision construing the ICPC.

Added In re R.W. and N.W., 2011 VT 124, 191 Vt. 108, 39 A.3d 682 (cluster 1043738) for OUT-01, OUT-04 and INP-08: found while closing OUT-04, which previously had a single case. Its holding — the State must prove the material change in circumstances by clear and convincing evidence, not a preponderance — is the mirror image of In re I.B. and In re B.C. on the temporary/permanent divide and belongs with the reunification-failure analysis at OUT-01. Its OUT-04 value is narrower and is flagged as such in the entry: footnote 3, applying 33 V.S.A. sec. 5103(c), states that family-division jurisdiction ends when the child turns eighteen. That is dictum in a footnote, and it is offered because Vermont has no holding on aging out at all.

Added Tina Stocker v. State of Vermont, 2021 VT 71 (cluster 5090886) for DEC-01, DEC-02, INP-10, FAIL-04, OUT-06 and PMC-04: the most consequential addition in this pass for anyone relying on Sabia. Stocker holds that under the statute as amended, the only DCF duty that will support a damages action is the sec. 4915 duty to record a report and make an initial validity determination; the Legislature foreclosed any private right of action for the conduct of assessments and investigations under secs. 4915a and 4915b, and that conduct is in any event discretionary and within sovereign immunity. Sabia (1995) must now be read through Stocker (2021); the brief previously presented Sabia's duty holding without this limit.

Added In re E.T.C., 141 Vt. 375, 449 A.2d 937 (1982) (cluster 8208589) for INP-03 and DEC-02: INP-03 (Law-Enforcement Referral) previously had a single case. E.T.C. is the foundational Vermont constitutional rule for police contact with children — the independent-interested-adult requirement under Chapter I, Article 10 — and it arose from state troopers questioning children in SRS custody at a state-contracted group home, holding that the home's director, who urged cooperation with police, could not serve as the independent adult.
